title: A Counterexample to Wall's D(2) Problem
main_claim: There is a finite 3-dimensional D(2) complex X (the finite plus construction of the presentation complex of P=<x1,a1,x2,a2,s | x1a1x1^-1=a1^4, x2a2x2^-1=a2^3, x1=a2^13, sx2s^-1=a1^5> along K=<<x1^2,x2^3>>) that is not homotopy equivalent to any finite 2-complex. The obstruction: on a finite 2-complex, if H_2(Y;C_rho)=0 then rho is trivial on all torsion. Here H_2(X;C_rho)=0, but rho(x1)=-1 and x1 has order 2 in G.
coverage: I read all four sections in full. (1) Tower obstruction, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 2.2: I checked the specialization D(z)|_{z=1}=D(1) and the full-rank argument over C(z). I checked the Euler-characteristic step chi(A_i)=-dim H_1<=0, which gives b1>=1. I checked that the lift exists because H_1(F) is finite, and that the lifted map stays simplicial with no re-subdivision. I checked that H_2 injects for subcomplexes when dim<=2, including inside the infinite cover. For the strict increase in simplex count: equal counts would give a simplicial isomorphism, hence a section of p_i, hence surjectivity of p_i on pi_1, which is impossible because the image is ker(phi_i). The count is bounded by s(F). As sanity checks, the corollary agrees with Swan-type Euler-characteristic counting for finite groups and with proper-power relators in one-relator groups. (2) Plus construction, Proposition 3.1: H_1 of the K-cover vanishes. H_2 surjects onto R^r. The splitting q∂3=id gives H^3(X;M)=0 for every M. The relative complex is contractible and the splitting is degreewise, so H_*(B;N)≅H_*(X;N). (3) Lemma 4.1, K perfect: I verified the identities t1=a2^26=[t2,a2] and s t2 s^-1=a1^15=[t1,a1]. I verified the module relations u1=(1-a2)u2 and s u2=(1-a1)u1, the norm-element arguments giving 26u1=0 and 15u2=0, and that gcd(15,26)=1. (4) In sympy I checked that the character satisfies all four relators, recomputed the Fox matrix at rho (it matches eq. 4.4 exactly), confirmed rank 4, and confirmed the x1,a1,x2,s minor equals -4(1-zeta^2)≠0. The left/right Fox convention does not matter, because the conjugate character gives the conjugate matrix. x1 has order exactly 2 in G because rho(x1)=-1.
